before:
Interstate 16 connects Savannah to Macon across about 166 miles of Central Georgia. It is a main truck route for freight from the Port of Savannah, the fastest-growing container port on the U.S. East Coast, and federal crash data recorded 66 deaths on I-16 statewide from 2020 through 2024 (NHTSA Fatality Analysis Reporting System).

The result: a relentless stream of tractor-trailers, container chassis, and heavy commercial vehicles mixing with commuter traffic through construction zones, narrow lanes, and congested interchanges. For Savannah-area residents, I-16 is not just a highway — it is the most likely place to be involved in a catastrophic truck crash.
after:

It is a main truck route for freight from the Port of Savannah, the fourth-busiest container port in the United States, and federal crash data recorded 66 deaths on I-16 statewide from 2020 through 2024 (NHTSA Fatality Analysis Reporting System).

The result: a relentless stream of tractor-trailers, container chassis, and heavy commercial vehicles mixing with commuter traffic through construction zones, narrow lanes, and congested interchanges. For Savannah-area residents, I-16 is not just a highway — it is one of the region's main truck corridors.

before:
GDOT is reconstructing the I-16/I-95 interchange and widening I-16 through Chatham County. The construction zone between Milepost 156 and MP 164 — intersecting with Pooler Parkway, I-95, Dean Forest Road, Chatham Parkway, and I-516 — creates:

  • Narrowed lanes that leave no room for error when a truck drifts
  • Temporary routes and lane shifts that confuse drivers
  • Speed differentials between construction-zone traffic (45 mph) and trucks entering from ramps
  • Concrete barriers that eliminate escape routes during emergencies
after:
GDOT has finished rebuilding the I-16/I-95 interchange and is widening I-16 between I-95 and I-516 in Chatham County. The work zone — through the interchanges at Dean Forest Road, Chatham Parkway, and I-516 — creates:

  • Narrowed lanes that leave no room for error when a truck drifts
  • Temporary routes and lane shifts that confuse drivers
  • Speed differentials between slowing work-zone traffic and trucks entering from ramps
  • Concrete barriers that eliminate escape routes during emergencies

before:
Outside of the Savannah metropolitan area, I-16 narrows to two lanes in each direction for most of its roughly 166-mile length. Passing a slow-moving truck requires using the left lane — the same lane used by oncoming traffic during crossover crashes and by other trucks attempting the same pass. Head-on and sideswipe crashes on these two-lane stretches are frequently fatal.

before:
Twiggs County (Milepost 40-60)

Rural, two-lane stretch where fatigue-related crashes peak. The January 2026 multi-semitrailer fatal crash occurred in this zone. Minimal lighting, long straight stretches, and sparse rest facilities create prime conditions for drowsy driving.
after:
Rural Middle Georgia (Twiggs to Laurens Counties)

A long rural stretch with two lanes in each direction. The January 2026 fatal chain-reaction crash happened here, in Bleckley County near the Twiggs County line. The only rest areas on I-16 are in Laurens County, near mileposts 44 and 46, so tired drivers have few places to stop on long, straight stretches.

  2. Call 911 — Georgia State Patrol responds to I-16 crashes. Request medical assistance.

before: Multiple parties may share liability: the truck driver (fatigue, distraction, impairment), the trucking company (negligent hiring, HOS pressure, poor maintenance), the cargo shipper (overweight or improperly loaded containers from the port), the truck or parts manufacturer (defective brakes, tires), and in construction zone crashes, potentially the construction contractor or GDOT.
after: Multiple parties may share liability: the truck driver (fatigue, distraction, impairment), the trucking company (negligent hiring, HOS pressure, poor maintenance), the cargo shipper (overweight or improperly loaded containers from the port), the truck or parts manufacturer (defective brakes, tires), and in construction zone crashes, potentially the construction contractor or GDOT. A claim against GDOT is a claim against the State, which requires written ante litem notice within 12 months (O.C.G.A. § 50-21-26).
